n: Continuing his answer to Peter, Jesus tells a parable about a landowner hiring workers for his vineyard at daybreak, around 6 a.m.

f.g: The owner of an estate.
A common image for God’s people or work.

n: He agrees to pay them a denarius for the day — the normal fair wage for a laborer.

f.g: A denarius, a Roman silver coin — a standard day’s wage.

n: Around 9 a.m. he sees others standing around in the marketplace, where day laborers waited to be hired.

f.g: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about 9 a.m.

n: He hires them without naming a wage, simply promising to pay what is right. They trust him and go.

f.g: Whatever is fair.

n: He does the same at noon and again at 3 p.m.

f.g: About noon and 3 p.m.

n: At 5 p.m., with just an hour left, he finds still more people with no work and asks why they’ve been idle all day.

f.g: About 5 p.m. — the origin of the phrase “at the eleventh hour.”

n: No one had hired them. He sends them into the vineyard too. In God’s work, latecomers are still welcomed.
At evening the owner has his manager pay everyone, starting with those hired last — as the law required, wages were paid daily.

f.g: A manager who handled the owner’s business.

n: The one-hour workers each receive a full day’s wage — remarkable generosity.

f.g: A full denarius for one hour of work.

n: The all-day workers expect more, but they receive exactly what they agreed to.

f.w: they supposed that they should have received more
f.g: Comparison turned their fair wage into a grievance.

n: They grumble against the owner.

f.g: murmured = grumbled, complained.
The master of the household.

n: Their complaint: the latecomers did one hour, yet they’re treated the same as those who sweated through the heat of the whole day.

f.g: wrought = worked.

f.w: the burden and heat of the day
f.g: The scorching midday heat; a hot east wind could make field work grueling.

n: The owner calls the complainer “friend” and points out that he was paid exactly what was agreed. No injustice was done.

f.w: Friend, I do thee no wrong

n: The owner chooses to be generous to the latecomers, and that is his right.

f.g: Take what is yours.

n: The real issue is envy: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” God’s grace to others takes nothing from us.

f.g: An idiom for envy or stinginess.

n: In God’s kingdom the last are first. Many are invited, but few respond and become chosen.

f.w: many be called, but few chosen

n: On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus takes the Twelve aside privately.

f.g: Jerusalem sits high in the hills, so travelers always went “up” to it.

n: For the third time, Jesus predicts what awaits him: betrayal to the religious leaders and a death sentence.

f.w: they shall condemn him to death

n: This time he gives details: he will be handed to Gentiles (the Romans), mocked, whipped, and crucified — then rise on the third day.

f.g: The first time Matthew records Jesus naming crucifixion as the manner of his death.

f.w: the third day he shall rise again

n: Right after this solemn prediction, the mother of James and John comes with her sons to ask a favor.

f.g: Possibly Salome, who may have been Mary’s sister — making James and John Jesus’s cousins.

n: She asks for her sons to have the highest places of honor in his kingdom, at his right and left.

f.g: The place of greatest honor and authority.

f.w: Grant that these my two sons may sit

n: Jesus says they don’t understand what they’re asking. Can they drink his “cup” of suffering? They confidently say yes.

f.w: the cup that I shall drink of
f.g: A symbol of suffering assigned by God.

n: They will share his suffering — James became the first apostle martyred, and John suffered much. But places of honor are the Father’s to give.

f.w: Ye shall drink indeed of my cup

n: The other ten apostles are angry with James and John — perhaps because they wanted those places themselves.

f.g: Anger at something felt to be unfair.

n: Jesus contrasts worldly rulers, who lord it over their subjects, with the way his kingdom works.

f.g: Rulers.

n: Among his followers, whoever wants to be great must serve others.

f.g: Greek diakonos — servant, attendant (root of “deacon”).

n: Whoever wants to be first must become a servant to all.

f.g: Greek doulos — a slave or bondservant.

n: Jesus himself is the model: he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom — the price paid to set many free.

f.g: ransom = the price paid to free a slave or captive.

n: Leaving Jericho on the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus is followed by a large crowd, likely fellow pilgrims heading to Passover.

f.g: An oasis city about 15 miles northeast of Jerusalem, some 3,000 feet lower in elevation.

n: Two blind men by the roadside shout to Jesus as the Son of David — the messianic King.

f.g: Mark and Luke focus on one; Mark names him Bartimaeus.

n: The crowd tells them to be quiet, but they cry out even louder. Persistent faith won’t be silenced.

f.g: Be quiet.

n: Jesus stops, calls them, and asks what they want — inviting them to put their faith into words.

f.w: What will ye that I shall do unto you?

n: They ask simply to see. Unlike James and John’s request for status, theirs is humble.

f.w: that our eyes may be opened

n: Moved with compassion, Jesus touches their eyes. They see at once — and use their new sight to follow him.
